quests.hint: Give your name in a full, friendly sentence, then add the classic 'nice to meet you' to close the greeting.
quests.explanation: Native speakers rarely say only their name. 'I'm Priya' plus 'Nice to meet you' is the standard two-part greeting: it gives information and shows you're glad to meet the person.
quests.situationText: A new neighbor has just moved into the flat across from yours. You meet in the corridor and she smiles and says hello. Your name is Priya.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hello! I'm Priya, I've just seen you moving in. Nice to meet you.
quests.correctAnswer: Hi, I'm Priya. Nice to meet you.
acceptedSynonyms: Hello, my name is Priya. Nice to meet you.
Hi there, I'm Priya. Pleased to meet you.
Nice to meet you. I'm Priya.
Hi, I'm Priya. Nice to meet you.

quests.hint: Country answers usually start with 'I'm from…'. You can add the city if you want to say more.
quests.explanation: 'Where are you from?' is answered with 'I'm from + place'. Adding a second detail, like your city, keeps the conversation moving instead of ending it with one word.
quests.situationText: It's the first day of an English class. The teacher looks at you and asks where you come from. You are from Sao Paulo, in Brazil.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'm from Brazil. I live in Sao Paulo.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm from Brazil, from Sao Paulo.
acceptedSynonyms: I come from Brazil. I'm from Sao Paulo.
I'm from Brazil, from Sao Paulo.
I'm from Sao Paulo, in Brazil.
I'm from Brazil, a city called Sao Paulo.

quests.hint: Adults you meet for the first time usually get a slightly more careful greeting. Use the person's title and last name.
quests.explanation: With a friend's parent, 'Mrs. Clarke' shows respect, while 'Hello' or 'Hi' is friendly without being stiff. Choosing the title is your first taste of register: who you are talking to changes your words.
quests.situationText: Your friend Dan invites you home and you meet his mother at the door. Her name is Mrs. Clarke.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hello, Mrs. Clarke. It's lovely to meet you. Dan talks about you a lot.
quests.correctAnswer: Hello, Mrs. Clarke. It's nice to meet you.
acceptedSynonyms: Hi, Mrs. Clarke. Nice to meet you.
Good afternoon, Mrs. Clarke. Pleased to meet you.
Hello Mrs. Clarke, it's a pleasure to meet you.
Hello, Mrs. Clarke. It's nice to meet you.

quests.hint: '..., please' is the easiest way to sound polite when you order. Say the number first, then the item.
quests.explanation: In shops, the pattern 'number + item + please' is short, clear, and polite. Nobody expects a long sentence when you are pointing at what you want.
quests.situationText: In a small bakery, you point at the croissants on the counter. You would like two of them.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, two croissants, please.
quests.correctAnswer: Two croissants, please.
acceptedSynonyms: Could I have two croissants, please?
Two croissants, please.
I'd like two croissants, please.
Can I get two croissants, please?

quests.hint: Give the drink first, then your two changes. Short sentences are fine.
quests.explanation: When you customize an order, say what you want, then what to change. 'No sugar' is complete on its own; you don't need 'I don't want any sugar'.
quests.situationText: You sit down at a cafe and the waiter asks what you would like to drink. You want tea with milk but no sugar.
quests.sampleAnswer: I'll have a tea with milk, please, and no sugar.
quests.correctAnswer: A tea with milk, please. No sugar.
acceptedSynonyms: Could I have a tea with milk, but no sugar, please?
Tea with milk and no sugar, please.
I'd like a tea with milk, no sugar, please.
A tea with milk, please. No sugar.

quests.hint: 'To take away' (or 'to go') tells the seller you won't eat here. Put it at the end of your order.
quests.explanation: Food sellers always need to know 'eat here or take away?'. Saying it in your first sentence saves a question and sounds confident. Both 'take away' and 'to go' are understood.
quests.situationText: It's late evening and you're at a street stall. You want a small portion of fries and you plan to eat them while walking home.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, can I get some small fries to go, please?
quests.correctAnswer: Can I have a small fries to take away, please?
acceptedSynonyms: A small portion of fries to go, please.
Can I have a small fries to take away, please?
I'll have small fries to take away, please.
Could I get a small order of fries to take away, please?

quests.hint: A quick 'Thanks' is enough for small favors, but add a little energy to your voice.
quests.explanation: For tiny kindnesses between strangers, a short thank-you is normal. Adding 'so much' or 'a lot' makes it warmer without becoming a long speech.
quests.situationText: You run toward the lift with a heavy shopping bag. A stranger inside holds the door so it doesn't close.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, thanks a lot!
quests.correctAnswer: Thanks so much!
acceptedSynonyms: Thanks so much!
Thank you, I really appreciate it.
Oh, thank you very much.
Thanks for holding it!

quests.hint: Say what you are thanking them for. Name the gift and add a feeling word.
quests.explanation: A specific thank-you ('thank you for the book') feels real, and 'I love it' shows you like it. General thanks alone can sound automatic.
quests.situationText: It's your birthday at work. A coworker hands you a wrapped gift. You open it and find a novel you wanted to read.
quests.sampleAnswer: Wow, thank you! I've wanted to read this for ages.
quests.correctAnswer: Thank you so much for the book. I love it!
acceptedSynonyms: Thanks a lot for the book. It's perfect!
Thank you for this lovely book. I really like it.
Thank you so much for the book. I love it!
Oh, thank you for the book! It's just what I wanted.

quests.hint: There is a special phrase for thanking a host. Think about 'having' someone and about the food.
quests.explanation: 'Thank you for having me' is what guests say when they leave someone's home. Praising something specific, like the dinner, shows you noticed the effort.
quests.situationText: You have finished dinner at your friend's family home and it is time to leave. The food was really good and they were very kind to you.
quests.sampleAnswer: Thanks so much for having me. Everything was delicious.
quests.correctAnswer: Thank you for having me. Dinner was delicious.
acceptedSynonyms: Thank you for having me. Dinner was delicious.
Thank you for inviting me. The food was really good.
Thanks for having me tonight. I loved the dinner.
It was a lovely evening, thank you. The dinner was delicious.

quests.hint: Say sorry first, then check the other person is okay. Speed matters here.
quests.explanation: When you bump into someone, a quick 'sorry' comes automatically, and asking 'Are you okay?' shows you care about the person, not just the mistake.
quests.situationText: You are walking fast on a busy street while looking at your phone and you hit an older man's shoulder.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh, I'm so sorry! Are you all right?
quests.correctAnswer: Oh, sorry! Are you okay?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry about that. Are you all right?
Oh, sorry! Are you okay?
I'm so sorry, I wasn't looking. Are you okay?
Oh no, sorry! Is your shoulder okay?

quests.hint: An apology sounds sincere when you add a short reason. Say the reason after sorry.
quests.explanation: 'Sorry I'm late' names the problem and 'I missed the bus' gives a short reason. A reason isn't an excuse; it tells the other person it wasn't disrespect.
quests.situationText: You promised to meet your friend Ana at a cinema at six, but you are ten minutes late because your bus didn't come.
quests.sampleAnswer: Ana, hi! Sorry I'm late. My bus never came.
quests.correctAnswer: Sorry I'm late. I missed the bus.
acceptedSynonyms: I'm so sorry I'm late. The bus was late.
Sorry to keep you waiting. My bus didn't come.
Sorry I'm late, Ana. I missed my bus.
Sorry I'm late. I missed the bus.

quests.hint: Good apologies come with an action. Offer to fix the problem.
quests.explanation: 'I'm sorry' expresses the feeling, but 'Let me get some tissues' does something about it. Offering to help repairs the situation, which people usually value more than repeated apologies.
quests.situationText: During a study session, you knock over your water bottle and it soaks a classmate's notebook.
quests.sampleAnswer: Oh no! I'm so sorry. Let me grab some tissues right now.
quests.correctAnswer: I'm so sorry. Let me get some tissues.
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry! I'll get some paper towels right away.
I'm so sorry. Let me get some tissues.
I'm really sorry about your notebook. Let me help you dry it.
Oh no, I'm so sorry. I'll clean it up now.

quests.hint: Ask them to say it again with 'Sorry, could you…'. It works on the phone and in person.
quests.explanation: Asking for repetition is normal and not rude. Starting with 'Sorry' lets the speaker know the problem is your hearing, not their fault.
quests.situationText: You are on the phone with a delivery company and the line is noisy. You didn't hear the last thing the woman said.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, the line is bad. Could you say that again?
quests.correctAnswer: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
Sorry, I didn't catch that. Could you repeat it?
Could you repeat that, please? I can't hear you well.
I'm sorry, could you say that one more time?

quests.hint: Ask for a speed change, not a new explanation. 'More slowly' is the key idea.
quests.explanation: Requesting 'more slowly' is more helpful than 'I don't understand' because the teacher knows exactly what to change. Adding 'please' keeps the request friendly.
quests.situationText: Your teacher is explaining homework very quickly and you are writing it down. You can't keep up.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, could you talk a little more slowly, please?
quests.correctAnswer: Could you speak more slowly, please?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, could you speak a bit slower?
Can you say it more slowly, please? I'm writing it down.
Could you speak more slowly, please?
Would you speak a little more slowly, please?

quests.hint: Two things are needed: a polite way to get their attention, and a question about what was said.
quests.explanation: You can ask a stranger for help with a missed announcement. 'Excuse me' opens the conversation, and 'what did they say?' names the exact information you need.
quests.situationText: At a train station, an announcement plays over the speakers, but you missed it. A woman next to you is waiting too.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, sorry, did you understand the announcement? What did it say?
quests.correctAnswer: Excuse me, did you hear that? What did they say?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, did you hear that? What did they say?
Sorry, I missed the announcement. What did they say?
Excuse me, do you know what the announcement said?
Excuse me, could you tell me what they just said?

quests.hint: 'Where's…?' is short and natural. Add 'Excuse me' first when speaking to a stranger.
quests.explanation: 'Where's the restroom?' is a complete question for a real situation. Contracting 'where is' to 'where's' sounds normal in everyday speech.
quests.situationText: You have just arrived at an airport after a long trip and you need the restroom. An airport worker is standing nearby.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, where are the restrooms?
quests.correctAnswer: Excuse me, where's the restroom?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, where are the restrooms?
Excuse me, where can I find the restroom?
Excuse me, where's the restroom?
Hi, could you tell me where the restroom is?

quests.hint: 'Do you know where…is?' is softer than a direct question. Use it when you don't know if the person can help.
quests.explanation: 'Do you know where…' gives the other person an easy way to say 'no' if they aren't sure. It's a common way to ask strangers, including staff who are busy.
quests.situationText: You're inside a big shopping mall and you need a pharmacy. You stop a security guard walking past.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, do you know where the pharmacy is?
quests.correctAnswer: Do you know where the pharmacy is?
acceptedSynonyms: Do you know where the pharmacy is?
Excuse me, is there a pharmacy in this mall?
Sorry, could you tell me where the pharmacy is?
Do you happen to know where I can find a pharmacy?

quests.hint: Ask whether something exists nearby before asking where exactly. Try 'Is there a…near here?'
quests.explanation: 'Is there a bus stop near here?' is useful when you don't know the area, because it asks for the existence and the location in one question. 'Near here' keeps the answer short.
quests.situationText: You come out of a small grocery store in a town you don't know. You need a bus stop, so you ask the shop assistant inside before leaving.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, is there a bus stop around here?
quests.correctAnswer: Is there a bus stop near here?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, is there a bus stop nearby?
Excuse me, where's the nearest bus stop?
Is there a bus stop near here?
Could you tell me if there's a bus stop near here?

quests.hint: For prices, 'How much is/are…?' is the key. Use 'are' with plural things like mangoes.
quests.explanation: 'How much are these?' is used for plural items. Pointing at the fruit and saying 'these' is completely normal, so you don't need to know more vocabulary.
quests.situationText: You are at a fruit market and want to know the price of the mangoes in front of you. There's no sign.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, what's the price of these mangoes?
quests.correctAnswer: How much are these mangoes?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, how much are the mangoes?
Sorry, what's the price of these mangoes?
How much do these mangoes cost?
How much are these mangoes?

quests.hint: With one item, use 'is' and point with 'this' or 'that'.
quests.explanation: 'How much is this jacket?' works in any shop when there's no price tag. If the item is far, use 'that' to signal distance.
quests.situationText: In a clothes shop, you see a jacket you like, but it has no price label. A shop assistant is folding shirts nearby.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, how much is this jacket?
quests.correctAnswer: How much is this jacket?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, how much does this jacket cost?
How much is this jacket?
Could you tell me the price of this jacket?
Excuse me, what's the price of this jacket?

quests.hint: Ask for the price before you get in. Use 'How much will it be…?' or 'How much does it cost…?'
quests.explanation: Asking a taxi driver about the price before the trip avoids surprises. 'How much will it be?' fits future things, and the destination gives the driver what he needs.
quests.situationText: You are at a taxi stand and want to go to the airport. Before getting in, you want to know the fare.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hello, how much will it be to the airport?
quests.correctAnswer: How much will it cost to go to the airport?
acceptedSynonyms: How much is it to the airport, please?
Could you tell me how much it is to the airport?
How much would a ride to the airport be?
How much will it cost to go to the airport?

quests.hint: A polite question about time starts with 'Excuse me'. 'Do you have the time?' is friendlier than 'What time?'
quests.explanation: 'Do you have the time?' is a standard way to ask strangers. It doesn't mean 'do you own time', it's a fixed phrase. Starting with 'Excuse me' shows you know you're interrupting.
quests.situationText: Your phone battery is dead and you need to know the time. You see a man sitting on a bench near you.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, sorry to bother you, what time is it?
quests.correctAnswer: Excuse me, do you have the time?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, do you know what time it is?
Excuse me, do you have the time?
Excuse me, could you tell me the time?
Hi, sorry to bother you, what time is it?

quests.hint: For opening hours, use 'What time do you close…?' and add a time word like 'today'.
quests.explanation: 'What time do you close?' is the standard question for opening hours. 'Today' matters because many places close earlier on certain days.
quests.situationText: You are at a small public library and you want to stay and study for a few hours. You ask the librarian about closing.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, when does the library close today?
quests.correctAnswer: What time do you close today?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, when does the library close today?
Could you tell me what time you close today?
What time does the library close today?
What time do you close today?

quests.hint: Confirm that you are in the right place before you wait. 'Is this…?' is a useful frame.
quests.explanation: Asking 'Is this the right platform for…?' checks your assumption. This is safer than guessing and shorter than describing your whole plan.
quests.situationText: You are at a busy train station. You think your train to Leeds leaves from platform 3, but you want to be sure. A staff member walks by.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, is this the right platform for the Leeds train?
quests.correctAnswer: Is this the right platform for the train to Leeds?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, does the Leeds train leave from this platform?
Is this the right platform for the train to Leeds?
Sorry, is platform 3 the one for Leeds?
Could you tell me if this is the platform for Leeds?

quests.hint: 'Could you pass…, please?' is the classic table request. Keep it short.
quests.explanation: A simple request at the table is 'Could you pass the...?' It is friendly among friends and family, and you don't have to explain why you need the item.
quests.situationText: You're having dinner at a friend's table and the salt is at the other end, out of your reach.
quests.sampleAnswer: Sorry, could you pass me the salt when you get a chance?
quests.correctAnswer: Could you pass the salt, please?
acceptedSynonyms: Could you pass the salt, please?
Can you pass me the salt, please?
Would you pass the salt, please?
Sorry, could I have the salt?

quests.hint: Use 'borrow' when you will return the item. Add 'for a minute' to show it's temporary.
quests.explanation: 'Borrow' means you'll return it. Saying 'for a minute' tells the person the favor is small, so it's easy to say yes.
quests.situationText: It's the beginning of an exam and you realize you left your pen at home. The student next to you has two.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, can I borrow your pen for a minute?
quests.correctAnswer: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, could I borrow one of your pens?
Do you have a spare pen I could borrow?
Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
Would you mind lending me a pen for a minute?

quests.hint: Give a short reason with the request. It makes the other person more willing to help.
quests.explanation: A request plus a short reason ('It's so hot') sounds fair and human. Without the reason, a request to a stranger can feel like an order.
quests.situationText: You're on a crowded bus without air conditioning. You're sitting next to a window, but a woman sits beside it and can reach the handle more easily.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, could you open the window, please? It's really hot in here.
quests.correctAnswer: Could you open the window, please? It's so hot.
acceptedSynonyms: Could you open the window, please? It's so hot.
Would you mind opening the window? It's very warm in here.
Sorry, could you open the window a little? It's hot.
Could you open the window, please? I'm feeling really hot.

quests.hint: Ask if the seat is free with a simple question. No need for a long sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Is this seat free?' or 'Is anyone sitting here?' is what people ask before sitting next to a stranger. Asking first is a basic social courtesy.
quests.situationText: You board a nearly full bus and see one empty seat next to a stranger who's looking out the window.
quests.sampleAnswer: Hi, is anyone sitting here?
quests.correctAnswer: Is this seat free?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, is anyone sitting here?
Is this seat free?
Do you mind if I sit here?
Is it okay if I sit here?

quests.hint: Permission questions use 'Is it okay if I…?' or 'Can I…?'. Mention exactly what you want to do.
quests.explanation: 'Is it okay if I charge my phone?' names the action, which lets the staff member answer 'yes' or 'no' easily. It also shows respect for their space.
quests.situationText: You're at a cafe and your phone battery is at 2 percent. There's a wall socket beside your table. The barista is free.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, is it okay if I plug in my phone here?
quests.correctAnswer: Is it okay if I charge my phone here?
acceptedSynonyms: Excuse me, can I charge my phone at this table?
Would it be all right if I charged my phone here?
Do you mind if I plug my phone in here?
Is it okay if I charge my phone here?

quests.hint: Rules differ from place to place, so ask 'Am I allowed to…?' when you aren't sure.
quests.explanation: 'Am I allowed to…?' is perfect when you are unsure about a rule. It's more polite than just doing it, and it protects you from a guard telling you off.
quests.situationText: You are in a museum and want to photograph a painting. You don't see any sign about photos. A guard stands nearby.
quests.sampleAnswer: Excuse me, am I allowed to take photos in this room?
quests.correctAnswer: Excuse me, am I allowed to take photos here?
acceptedSynonyms: Sorry, can I take pictures in here?
Excuse me, am I allowed to take photos here?
Excuse me, is photography allowed in this room?
Is it okay to take photos of the paintings?
